title: Who am I?
hookLine: Ramana Maharshi taught self-enquiry: ask "who am I?" and trace the "I" to its source

cards: A clinic intake form asks who you are, in pieces. Name. Address.
Each box is small, and each answer is true. Fill them all in and you've described a person well enough to be treated, billed and called back.
In South India, at the foot of a hill called Arunachala, a quiet teacher named Ramana Maharshi asked the same question with no boxes at all. He didn't want it filled in.

teach.b: Ramana's teaching survives in short works and in conversations his visitors wrote down. One small booklet carries the question as its title: in Tamil, Nan Yar, who am I?
This is a paraphrase, not his words, but the method goes like this. Every thought you have is somebody's thought. Before the worry, before the plan, there is an I that has it.
In Ramana's account, that sense of I is the first thought, and every other thought rises after it. So when a thought comes, don't follow it out into the world.
Turn it around: to whom did this come? To me. And who am I?
Not a riddle to solve with words.

teach.h: NOT THE BODY, NOT THE MIND.
teach.b: Ramana goes through the obvious answers: not the body, not the senses, not even the thinking mind. One way readers put it: each of these can be noticed, and the I is the one noticing.
The point is to keep attention on the I itself, and trace it back toward where it rises. He gives a striking picture for what the question does.

teach.h: THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE.
teach.b: At a cremation, someone stirs the fire with a stick, keeping it burning. At the end, the stick goes into the fire too.
The question works on all the other thoughts like that stick, he says, and in the end it burns up as well. Then the asking stops, and what remains is not another thought. Yesterday a room sang names.
Today, a single word, I, followed home.

how: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-enquiry by meeting each thought with the question "to whom did this come?" and turning attention back to the sense of I, in sitting practice and through the day.

o: tracing each thought back to the one who has it
listing your roles until you find the true one
a riddle a teacher asks to test a new student

s: Ramana wanted a careful list of answers to who am I
the question is meant to be followed, not filled in. the obvious answers are set aside.
Ramana's method meets each thought by asking to whom it came
to me. and who am I? attention turns back to the I itself.
in Ramana's picture, the question itself burns up in the end
like the stick that stirs a cremation fire and goes into it at the end.

games.q: in the middle of your sit, a thought shows up: I'm bad at this. what does Ramana's method do?
o: argue with it until it goes away.
follow it to see where it leads.
ask: to whom did this come?
games.why: to me. and who am I? the thought isn't fought or followed. attention turns back toward the I that had it.

practice: Ask "who am I?" once, inside, slowly, and wait without answering in words; if an answer shows up anyway, a job, a name, a mood, ask: to whom did this come?
Ask again with a longer silence, and a third time with the longest silence of all. You're not looking for a reply, only at where the question lands.
